childNodes.textContent: We transfer paintings by masters into color paper, in order to identify their color instrumentation.

Start with one of these painted stand-ins, or bring a reproduction of a painting you love. The screen sorts every pixel into a few flat papers. Albers wanted the climate of a painting, not its details, so fewer papers is often truer.

childNodes.textContent: We try to give a general impression only as to climate, temperature, aroma, or sound of their work—not minute details.

The same papers, sized by how much of the painting each one covers. This is the painter's instrumentation, which colours and how much of each. Try two papers, then sixteen, and see when the climate of the painting arrives.

childNodes.textContent: It is another means of learning to develop a sensitive and critical eye for color relatedness.

A machine picks the colours that cover the most. A painter might pick a small yellow that carries the whole picture. Albers' students worked from a box of papers, not from the painting. Tap the painting to look closely at a spot, then choose the nearest paper from the collection. You will rarely find an exact match. Aim for the climate, not the details.

childNodes.textContent: Five or six papers are often enough to bring back a painting's climate
How much of each colour there is matters as much as which colours they are
Clustering picks the colours that cover the most. A painter would also keep the small accent that carries the picture
Flat papers take away the brushwork and leave only the colour decisions
Matching from a limited collection, not an eyedropper, is what trains the eye for climate
Pulling a palette from an image by area misses the accents, so tune extracted palettes by eye
